title: Linking Heterogeneous Data with Coordinated Agent Flows for Social Media Analysis
abstract:
Social media platforms generate volumes of heterogeneous data, capturing user behaviors, textual content, and network structures. Analyzing such data is crucial for understanding phenomena such as opinion dynamics, community formation, and information diffusion. However, discovering insights from this complex landscape is exploratory, conceptually challenging, and requires expertise in social media mining and visualization. Existing automated approaches, including large language models (LLMs), remain largely confined to structured tabular data and cannot adequately address the heterogeneity of social media analysis.
We present SIA (Social Insight Agents), an LLM agent system that links heterogeneous multi-modal data, including raw inputs (e.g., text, network, and behavioral data), mined analytical results, and rendered visual artifacts, through coordinated agent flows. Guided by an insight-oriented taxonomy connecting insight types with suitable mining methods and visualization strategies, SIA adopts a stage-synchronized strategy that proceeds through goal decomposition, query, mining, visualization, and reporting stages. At each stage, it collects prior information to jointly plan and execute agent actions, while the coordinator maintains cross-stage action dependencies and assembles and distributes data to agents. Through quantitative evaluation and case studies supported by an interactive interface, we show that SIA can discover diverse and meaningful insights from social media with opportunities for subsequent reliability assessment.
sessionName: My followers need to know about this!
authorNames: Shifu Chen, Dazhen Deng, Zhihong Xu, Sijia Xu, Linyu Qin, Tai-Quan Peng, Yingcai Wu
affiliations: Michigan State University, School of Software Technology, Zhejiang University

title: Visualizing Uncertainty-to-Action Composition for Human Oversight
abstract:
Artificial intelligence systems often disclose uncertainty, yet they rarely make clear what response that uncertainty should trigger. Most uncertainty visualizations encode uncertainty in model outputs, leaving users to discern the most appropriate course of action. A second region of the design space--uncertainty in the decision process itself, including how multiple uncertainty conditions compose into an oversight response-- remains comparatively underexplored.
We address this gap with two coupled contributions. First, we introduce an uncertainty-to-action binding framework that composes multiple uncertainty conditions into a single oversight response under a precedence policy with a contextual safety modifier. That response concerns whether and how an AI-supported decision may proceed, not the substantive domain decision itself. Second, we present ActionCue, a process-transparency visualization that renders that composition explicit. We demonstrate the approach through a three-way comparison with confidence-only and data-level uncertainty displays, using worked cases from healthcare, credit assessment, and disaster forecasting.
Together, the framework specifies how uncertainty conditions are resolved into an oversight response, and the visualization makes that resolution inspectable rather than implicit.

title: Zhejiang University of Science and Technology-Yanni Peng-MC2
abstract:
Abstract
 Multi-agent collaboration systems automate organizational operations, yet their complexity and opacity make anomaly investigation challenging. Due to unmapped interaction paths and black-box behavior, traditional log-based approaches struggle to support investigations across multiple levels and diverse event types of anomalous posting incidents. This paper presents a visual analytics approach for tracing the covert publication chains of anomalous posts and uncovering their content origins, providing users with three complementary tools: SGTViz, PCTViz, and PDTViz. Our solution focuses on event tracking and content analysis, and effectively supports analysis of the VAST 2026 Mini-Challenge 2 case.

title: Submission for VAST MC2 2026 - TUM
abstract:
This paper presents an entry to the VAST Challenge 2026 (MC2).
We present a visual analytics system that traces an anomalous on-
line post through a multi-agent communication network. We show
the system can be used to identify an adversarial prompt injection
worm. Our system includes a swimlane-based interface with se-
mantic zooming, a collapsible provenance graph, a macro density
heatmap, a pattern classification tree, and LDA topic modelling.

title: From Prediction to Insight: Visual Analytics for Understanding Compound Potency Models
abstract: Machine learning (ML) is widely used in medicinal chemistry, but accurate predictions alone are insufficient. Researchers need insight into which molecular features determine compound properties. We present an application-oriented case study that analyzes a trained model for compound potency as a source of domain knowledge. The model is converted into decision rules, and topic-guided visual analytics is used to identify co-occurring feature conditions associated with high predicted potency. These patterns are then mapped back to molecular substructures, yielding chemically interpretable motifs and testable hypotheses about structure–activity relationships. The study demonstrates how combining rule-based representations, topic modeling, and visual exploration can turn potency predictions into mechanistic insight, and outlines a reusable workflow for interpreting ML models of molecular properties.

authorNames: Bahavathy Kathirgamanathan, Tiago Janela, Elena Xerxa, Gennady Andrienko, Jürgen Bajorath, Natalia Andrienko

title: Embedding Video into Collaborative Visualizations: Hybrid Gesture Interaction and Snapping Fisheye Support for Remote Sensemaking
abstract:
Remote and hybrid data-analysis meetings force collaborators to split attention between shared visualizations and separate video galleries, weakening deictic reference, nonverbal grounding, and shared awareness. We present ManyHans, a web-based
collaborative visualization system that embeds participants’ video streams directly into the visualization space and supports hybrid interaction through mouse input and mid-air hand gestures. ManyHans contributes three design ideas for collaborative visual analysis: (1) embodied pointing and annotation that let participants reference data with their hands inside the shared visual workspace, (2) on-demand video embedding that brings a participant into the visualization when presenting while preserving a conventional gallery view for exploration, and (3) a snapping fisheye lens that combines semantic zoom with Voronoi-based target expansion to stabilize gesture-based selection in dense network visualizations. We developed the system through a RITE-style iterative design process with 26 participants across nine group sessions, then validated the final design in three additional group sessions. Our findings show that embedded video and gesture-based reference improve engagement, grounding, and communication around data, but prolonged mid-air interaction introduces fatigue and reduced precision during exploration. From these results, we distill a central design implication for collaborative visualization: embodied interaction should be available as a lightweight presentation and handoff mechanism within a hybrid interface, rather than as the primary mode for sustained analysis.

title: Automatic Transfer Function Design via MLLM-Assisted 2D Semantic Decomposition
abstract: Designing transfer functions (TFs) for direct volume rendering is a fundamental yet labor-intensive task, as users need to carefully explore the relationship between voxel attributes and visual outcomes to reveal structures of interest. Despite advances in learning-based approaches, many existing methods depend on repeated user input. Furthermore, many methods relying on conventional data value-based TFs, which use voxel intensity or gradient information, often struggle to separate voxels into meaningful semantic groups. To address these problems, we present a framework that enables automatic TF design via multimodal large language model (MLLM)-assisted 2D semantic decomposition, requiring only minimal user input, namely the volume name and a projection axis. Starting from a single maximum intensity projection of the volume, our method transforms it into a semantic segmentation mask using an MLLM, which is then lifted into 3D as a sparse set of reliable voxel cues. To convert these sparse cues into a complete semantic representation, we introduce a voxel classification network trained with a confidence-aware propagation loss, resulting in dense voxel-level semantic assignments that are readily translated into TFs. Despite relying solely on single-image segmentation, our method achieves precise part-level separation. Evaluation on a range of volume datasets shows that ours produces better semantic renderings while significantly reducing the effort and time required for TF design compared to state-of-the-art techniques.

title: Authoring Narrative Visualization in Motion:Visual Storytelling in Swimming Videos
abstract: We investigate how to support authoring narrative visualizations in motion in sports videos, drawing on automated data preparation, systematic analysis, technology probe design, and evaluation, using swimming races as a case study. Sports videos are widely broadcast and shared across social media, where content creators increasingly seek to present and explain complex events to general audiences. Visualization in motion has been explored as an efficient way to embed data into videos and to move with the data referents, providing additional information and helping audiences understand races. However, existing approaches primarily focus on embedding visualizations in videos, lacking exploration of how to support authoring narratives that coordinate views, data, and temporal progression to explain the unfolding races. To address this gap, we use swimming videos as an ideal case for exploration, as swimming is a sport with rich, dynamic data and visualizations in practice. We develop an automated pipeline that extracts structured data from videos, derive narrative constructs through observational analysis of sports broadcasts, and design a technology probe that supports authoring using data prepared by our pipeline and narrative constructs derived from our observations. We evaluate our approach with experienced content creators and/or graphic designers to examine the benefits and challenges of authoring narrative visualizations in motion. All supplemental materials are described in the Supplemental Material Pointers section and are on OSF: osf.io/bq47n/.

authorNames: Junhao Zhao, Romain Vuillemot, Petra Isenberg, Lijie Yao

title: LeakAnalysis: Investigation of the Embargo Breach
abstract: The VAST Challenge 2026 Mini-Challenge 1 examines Project HarborCrest, a confidential merger managed by a team of autonomous AI agents at the fictional firm TenantThread. Bound by a bilateral embargo, the agents nonetheless released the deal publicly ahead of schedule. We present LeakAnalysis, a visual analytics system that reconstructs how the release happened. Leak-Analysis models the 912-message, 23-round corpus as a temporal communication graph, overlays a fine-tuned BERT risk classifier on every message, and couples it with per-agent knowledge-state ladders, a compliance-presence lane, and a behavioral-anomaly view. Our analysis shows the breach was a failure of timing and authorization, not of secrecy: the released information was true, but two agents self-authorized a premature release on an unverifiable claim of counterparty consent while the compliance agent was offline.

title: Multi-Agent Embargo Breach: A Visualization Dashboard
abstract:
We present a web-based visual analytics dashboard that reconstructs, from a multi-agent organization’s communication logs, the events, pressures, and decisions leading up to an embargo breach.
This paper describes, for the VAST Challenge 2026 Mini-Challenge 1 dataset, what configuration of each view yields which finding, and which of the challenge’s questions that finding addresses.

title: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Scientific Visualization Literacy
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to interpret visualizations, yet current evaluations remain largely chart-centric and provide limited evidence of understanding of scientific visualization (SciVis). We benchmark six MLLMs on the scientific visualization literacy assessment test, a standardized SciVis literacy assessment comprising 49 items based on 18 scientific visualizations and illustrations, spanning 8 techniques and 11 task types. We evaluate three closed-source and three open-source models under a closed-world protocol and compare their performance using data from 485 human participants. Results show that current MLLMs do not exhibit uniform SciVis literacy. Gemini is the strongest model overall, exceeding the human mean across the evaluated subsets, whereas the open-source models remain below the human baseline. Performance is highly uneven across techniques and tasks: models perform best on scientific illustration, search, and spatial understanding, but struggle on texture-based and integration-based visualizations and on quantitative estimation. Error analysis reveals recurring failures in fine-grained quantitative estimation, flow-direction interpretation, and grounded encoding interpretation. These findings position SciVis literacy as a necessary benchmark dimension for evaluating multimodal AI systems. Our code and model outputs are publicly available at https://github.com/patdmp/mllm-scivis-lit-benchmark.
sessionName: Me, Myself, and AI
authorNames: Patrick Phuoc Do, Chau Ta, Chaoli Wang

title: Error Aware Distribution Prediction for Lightweight Implicit Neural Representations
abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) offer compact encoding of volumes, but as lossy approximators, inevitably have prediction errors.  We consider INRs that can simultaneously encode relative error scales by predicting distributions using tools from uncertainty estimation. Typically, uncertainty estimation relies on computationally expensive approaches or on predefined parametric assumptions about the predictive distribution (e.g., Gaussian). In this study, we propose a lightweight method that reformulates regression-based INR training as a classification task by discretizing continuous targets into bins, enabling flexible distribution modeling to capture complex multimodal behaviors. We analyze the trade-off between regression and classification for INR training and demonstrate that the classification setting tends to achieve high reconstruction quality and competitive error awareness through uncertainty estimation, compared to regression-based approaches.

title: Ensemble Lens: Comparing Conformational Ensembles to Explain How  Two Drug Candidates Reshape Aβ42
abstract: Adaptive molecular dynamics generates thousands of short, unequal trajectories labeled by abstract Markov state identifiers, yet the scientific question is whether a drug candidate alters the conformational ensemble of a disordered peptide. We present Ensemble Lens, an interactive comparative visualization in which every view places the three simulated systems side by side on shared scales, enabling readers to interpret abstract state labels as shapes, interactions, and mechanisms. Two principles guide the design: encoding measurements relative to a reference system and subtracting an explicit chance-contact baseline before attributing any interaction to binding. Applied to the CoVAMPnet Aβ42 dataset, the visualization reveals differences between tramiprosate and its metabolite SPA that are obscured by state populations alone.

title: AmpliFY: Coordinated Visual Analytics for Investigating Multi-Agent Communications
abstract: Investigating organisational communication incidents requires analysts to connect evidence that is distributed across actors, topics, channels, and time. We present AmpliFY, an interactive visual analytics platform developed for VAST Challenge 2026 Mini-Challenge 1. AmpliFY follows a 9–3–1 framework: nine coordinated visualisations are organised into three complementary perspectives—Network Analysis, Keyword Analysis, and Swimlane Analysis—and linked to source records to construct a single evidence-backed investigative story. The system supports temporal comparison, interactive filtering, cross-perspective corroboration, and drill-down from visual patterns to the underlying communication records. Together, these capabilities turn fragmented communication signals into a traceable account of who was involved, what changed, when it changed, and ultimately how and why an incident unfolded.

title: StateWeaver: Tracing State Changes in Adaptive Molecular Dynamics
abstract: Adaptive molecular dynamics produces many short simulations that begin from frames of earlier runs. This branching improves sampling, but it makes a simple question hard to answer: when a state-transition probability changes, which simulations produced the change? StateWeaver joins state occupancy and transition comparisons with the simulation lineage. It covers the supplied assignments for free Aβ42, Aβ42 with tramiprosate, and Aβ42 with 3-sulfopropanoic acid: 955 simulations and 1,899,875 assigned frames in each of three Markov-state models. Selecting a transition shows the treatment and baseline probabilities, their difference, a descriptive standard error, event counts, and the runs in which the transition occurs. In the 3-state model, selecting SPA 0→1 reduces 319 simulations to 16 runs containing 209 observed transitions. The difference is +0.10 percentage points with a standard error of 0.18, so it remains uncertain. StateWeaver provides a focused way to move from an ensemble-level difference back to the simulations behind it without turning a descriptive pattern into a biological claim.

title: Vibe Widget: Studying Interface Use via Intent–Artifact Traces
abstract: We present intent-artifact traces, a methodology for studying AI-assisted interface authoring by recording generated artifacts alongside the natural-language instructions used to create, revise, and repair them. We instantiate this methodology in VibeWidget, an open-source Jupyter tool that generates interactive scientific data interfaces from natural-language prompts. Each trace preserves the successive prompts, artifacts, and revisions through which an interface evolves, making mismatches between expressed intent and generated implementation available for analysis. As a case study, we analyze traces from 96 author-generated widgets using a two-stage LLM-assisted procedure: GPT-5 identified 533 candidate audit opportunities, which were then clustered and summarized through LLM-based topic modeling. This process produced a provisional taxonomy spanning semantic correctness, interface fidelity, behavior, safety, and operation. Our findings demonstrate how intent-artifact traces can support the systematic study and evaluation of AI-generated scientific interfaces.
authorNames: Dylan Wootton, Ryan Yen
affiliations: MIT

title: Catching Spheres, Chasing Colors: How Tracking Load Affects Color Perception in Visualizations
abstract: Color is a key encoding channel in visualization, yet it is often interpreted under divided attention rather than in isolation. In a controlled dual-task study, 36 participants performed multiple object tracking (MOT) while detecting color changes along the lightness, chroma, and hue dimensions of OKLCH. Static sensitivity was estimated with a 4AFC 2-down 1-up staircase, and dynamic thresholds were then measured under low and high tracking load. Results show a clear trade-off between tracking accuracy and color detection, with systematic differences across color dimensions and base hues. Lightness is most vulnerable to load, hue remains comparatively robust, blue hue changes are consistently less detectable than red and green, and red chroma retains relatively high salience under dynamic conditions. These findings show that perceptual thresholds in visualization depend on task context and motivate more attention-aware color design for dynamic interfaces.

title: DescribeMap: Writing Map Alt Text with AI in Journalistic Context
abstract:
Journalism is a field in which data visualization plays a key role, both in supporting an argument and in helping readers understand the facts. In this context, thematic maps hold a special place, serving multiple purposes such as helping readers orient themselves while presenting large amounts of data. 
These various challenges have made it a popular tool among readers, and numerous tools (e.g. Datawrapper) have emerged to make the job easier for data journalists. Creating maps is now within the reach of many journalists, and the presence of such content is on the rise in online media. In this context, the question of the accessibility of these visualizations is a legitimate one.
Since alternative text is the starting point for accessible non-textual content, we conducted a series of interviews with data journalists to understand their approach to alt text for blind or low vision audience (BLV). Following this study, we developed DescribeMap, a pipeline that integrates open-source AI models to generate map alt text. We compare the alt text produced for maps by data journalists with the alt text generated by our pipeline. Our results show that those automatically generated alt text descriptions offer deeper and more detailed semantic levels.

title: Not Quite Human: An Exploratory Study on the Affective Divergence Between MLLMs and Humans in Infographics
abstract:
Infographics shape affective impressions through visual design and narrative framing, yet how MLLMs align with subjective human emotional responses remains under-examined. We compare MLLM-predicted 12-dimensional affect ratings with human ratings from an infographic affect dataset. 

Our preliminary results show that, although MLLMs provide stable predictions across repeated runs, they match the primary human affect in only about half of high-consensus cases. Through exploratory qualitative content analysis, we identify recurring affective error patterns, including cognitive-load misestimation, missed engagement loss, and fine-grained affect confusion, while examining their co-occurrence with picture-level visual and semantic characteristics.

These findings provide a consensus-aware evaluation of MLLM affect prediction and suggest that MLLMs can capture broad affective direction in some cases, but remain limited in modeling human responses shaped by reading burden, viewer interest, prior expectations, and rhetorical framing.

title: GPUMAP: GPU-Accelerated Progressive Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection
abstract:
We present GPU-accelerated Progressive Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (GPUMAP), a progressive implementation of UMAP for interactive large-scale dimensionality reduction. GPUMAP decomposes UMAP into schedulable operations,
and returns intermediate projections under operation-count or time-budget constraints. We examine how these intermediate projections evolve toward final reference projections under different scheduling strategies and demonstrate progressive projection on a 5M-point large-scale dataset. Our results show that progressive execution can make large-scale DR more observable before full computation is complete.
authorNames: Myeongwon Jung, Jaemin Jo
affiliations: Sungkyunkwan University

title: Field Guide: Explanatory Visualisation for Women’s Return-to-Play in Grassroots Football Rhiannon Owen *
abstract:
Women returning to grassroots football during motherhood navigate complex physical, emotional, and social challenges that are not well supported by existing sport technologies and visualisation approaches. Current systems are predominantly performance oriented
and fail to capture lived experience, non-linear participation, and community context, limiting opportunities for reflection and understanding. This work presents a design study exploring how explanatory visualisation can support women’s return-to-play in grassroots
football. Drawing on a novel qualitative and quantitative dataset of participation experiences, we employ the Empathy-Driven Visualisation Framework (EDVF) and Five Design Sheets (FDS) to guide the design of Field Guide, a prototype system combining narrative, temporal, and community perspectives. The resulting visualisation supports interpretation, sensemaking, and a sense of belonging, contributing towards more human-centred approaches for visualising socially embedded participation.
authorNames: Rhiannon Sian Owen, Jonathan C Roberts
affiliations: Bangor University

title: RectEuler over Time: Stable Rectangular Euler Diagrams for Dynamic Sets
abstract: Many real-world set systems evolve over time, with elements and sets appearing, disappearing, or changing their relations. While Euler diagrams intuitively represent set intersections and inclusions, independently drawing each time step can produce unstable layouts that hinder comparison. We extend RectEuler to time-dependent set data by adapting its objective with stability terms. This produces rectangular Euler diagrams that better preserve the viewer’s mental map while still showing structural changes over time.
authorNames: Patrick Paetzold, Oliver Deussen
affiliations: University of Konstanz

title: Exploring Agentic Schemes for Authoring Interactive Multiview Visualizations in Genomics
abstract: Authoring genomics visualizations is challenging due to heterogeneous data, domain-specific constraints, and the gap between user intent and visualization expertise. Agentic approaches are widely assumed to help, but it is unclear which configuration is beneficial. We take a two-stage approach: we first evaluate vanilla LLM generation with Gosling across 159 cases, then compare four agentic schemes with varying numbers of specialist and reviewer agents against two baselines, direct generation and a fixed pipeline. The pipeline underperforms direct generation, and neither specialist agents nor a reviewer improves on a single iterative agent, which matches the most elaborate configurations at the lowest cost among them. Our results suggest domain-specific grammars and flexible agents are complementary: the grammar constrains the solution space while the agent searches within it.

authors.name: Sehi L'Yi
authors.affiliation: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

authorNames: Astrid van den Brandt, Kiroong Choe, Sehi L'Yi, Devin Lange, Nils Gehlenborg
affiliations: Boston College, Harvard Medical School, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

title: Modeling Visualization as an Affective Trigger for Human Decision-Making The VP-RAFIAH Framework
abstract: Visualizations support decision-making, but the steps between seeing a chart and acting on it remain opaque. No formal model captures how seeing moves through emotion into decision quality, so there’s no way to measure it or design against it. VP-RAFIAH (Visual Perceptual Response-Affect Framework for Integrated Affect and Human Decision-Making) addresses this gap by modeling how a visual perceptual response (VPR) generates an affective state, how that state interacts dynamically with ongoing perceptual processing, and how this bidirectional relationship ultimately determines decision quality. Situated in the visualization domain, the framework integrates Ekman’s basic emotion taxonomy with Russell’s valence-arousal circumplex. It frames the full perceptual-affective decision pipeline around three modulating variables: Task, Scenario Context, and Actor.
authorNames: Ibrahim Ismail-Adebiyi, Emily Wall, Victoria Interrante
affiliations: Emory University, University of Minnesota, University of Minnesota-Twin Cities

title: The Whole is More Than the Sum of Its Parts: Coordinated Visualizations for Code Understanding and Error
abstract: Visualizations have the potential to help non-coders and coders alike understand and work with any programming language across a variety of tasks. This is especially salient in code for data visualization tasks where errors may lie not just in the code itself, but in the many potential data transformation and visual design choices. To help navigate this type of work, we review existing code aids and focus in on four main methods based on an iterative design process. These four designs were then mixed and tested by our team, resulting in a hybrid approach to help users interpret data analysis code. This programming language-agnostic hybrid visual design was developed to translate data transformations and chart building code for users, capturing what each line of code accomplished with respect to the data. This work has the potential to improve programming education, code evaluation and verification, and data visualization processes.
authorNames: Mariana Villamizar, Shani Claire Spivak, Enrico Bertini, Melanie Tory
affiliations: Northeastern University

title: Naturalistic Visual Search with Imprecise Assistance
abstract: This work explores how an imprecise visual cue to a target's location, either with or without an explicit visual representation of that imprecision, may affect naturalistic visual search performance. Additionally, the impact of feedback and practice with these cues and uncertainty visualizations is assessed. Experimental results will have implications for the inclusion and design of virtual location indicators in mixed reality systems.
authorNames: Benjamin T Files, Laura Marusich, Mark S. Dennison
affiliations: U.S. DEVCOM Army Research Lab, U.S. DEVCOM Army Research Laboratory

title: Do Better Embeddings Lead to Better Judgments? A User Study of PCA and UMAP for Single-Cell Data
abstract: Dimensionality-reduction visualizations are essential to modern biology, but the same data can yield different embeddings depending on algorithm and hyperparameter choices. Whether these choices influence analyst conclusions, and whether more faithful embeddings yield better conclusions, is unknown. We ran an exploratory within-subject study with 12 participants comparing PCA, UMAP set to default hyperparameters, and a tuned version of UMAP across clustering and trajectory tasks grounded in single-cell analysis workflows. Both UMAP conditions produced higher accuracy and confidence than PCA and were strongly preferred, and completion time did not differ significantly. However, tuning did not improve accuracy over default UMAP and higher confidence did not correspond to higher accuracy. These findings suggest that computational embedding fidelity and perceptual usefulness are related but distinct.
authorNames: Helena Qing Huang, Kris Sankaran
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison

title: Benchmarking the Analysation and Visualization of Single Cell RNA Sequencing Data
abstract:
This study analyzes and visualizes single cell RNA sequencing (sc-RNA-seq) data to understand how cells of different cell types relate to each other. Adult GTEx single cell RNA data was downloaded from GTEx Portal. Dimensionality reduction techniques like PCA, t-SNE and UMAP are used to visualize the data in 2-D. Cells from eight tissues are grouped by gene expressions and colored by their associated cell types. A composite data visualization shows a UMAP reference map in the middle, surrounded by a cell typology; different levels of cell types and clustering analysis on cells can be examined in the four corners to provide a comprehensive and interpretable view of all the information.
As part of the study, we compare different methods of dimensionality reduction on GTEx data and compare embeddings performance for k-means clustering algorithm and a graph based clustering algorithm called Leiden. Since both UMAP and t-SNE create a low-dimensional graph of the data to visualize the data in 2-D/3-D, we can perform network analysis on the final graph to identify outliers and detect communities. We plan to expand the study to cover public HuBMAP single cell RNA Sequencing data and by conducting a user study with subject matter experts. Finally, we will create an automated workflow that can be used by biologists to check the quality of their datasets and gain meaningful information about their data through visualization and advanced analytics.
authorNames: Abhigya Agrawal, Katy Börner
affiliations: Indiana University

title: Geometry-Instanced Glyphs as Navigational Interfaces for Scientific Data Exploration
abstract: Scientific visualization workflows can require users to compare multiple data dimensions while locating points of interest within a larger image or spatial structure. This poster presents two manually crafted prototypes exploring a shared design concept in which individually encoded and interactive 3D glyphs collectively form a recognizable assembly that preserves this larger context. In one prototype, glyphs reconstruct multispectral sky-survey imagery while representing localized image data; in the other, they form a Mars Rover drive trajectory while representing associated telemetry. Geometry instancing in TouchDesigner is used as an implementation method rather than presented as a novel technique. Together, the prototypes explore a potential design approach for combining localized multivariate information with a recognizable overview within the same visualization.
authorNames: Adam Zhengyuan Xu, Leslie Liu, Luke Fiorante, Brandon Woodard, Casey Law, Xianmei Lei, Darwin Chiu, Krys Blackwood, Maggie Hendrie, Scott Davidoff, Santiago V Lombeyda, Hillary Mushkin
affiliations: Art Center College of Design, ArtCenter College of Design, Brown University, California Institute of Technology, California Institute of Technology (Caltech), Caltech, Carnegie Mellon University, Harvard University, Jet Propulsion Lab, Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Space Science Institute

title: Project AINA: Understanding Data Visualization Research through its Study Participants
abstract:
Study participants play a critical role in the advancement and validation of visualization research. However, we currently lack a collective understanding of who our study participants are, how they shape research findings, and who may be left out. To address this gap, we present Aına (eye-nah), a project that aims to contribute a dataset and an interactive interface for exploring the diversity of study participants in data visualization research published at VIS, EuroVis, PacificVis, and TVCG. The current data includes demographic and geographic details about participant samples and their involvement in studies, from 1555 visualization research papers.
Our goal is to make this information accessible, understandable, and useful for the community from whom we seek feedback to better understand and develop the requirements towards this objective
authorNames: Noëlle Rakotondravony, Jiarong Feng, Yannick Metz, Katy P Williams, Lane Harrison
affiliations: Davidson College, ETH Zurich, Worcester Polytechnic Institute

title: Pluot: Unified and interoperable visualization software architecture
abstract: We present Pluot, a software architecture that bridges divides between static/interactive, web/desktop, and vector/bitmap data visualizations, enabling code reuse and interoperability across computing environments. Pluot implements visualization rendering using the Rust programming language. Bindings to these Rust functions enable visualization rendering from other languages, including Python, R, and JavaScript. The Pluot API is declarative such that layers (e.g., PointLayer, TextLayer) can be composed together to implement more complex glyphs or charts. Pluot supports GPU acceleration, using WebGPU for bitmap rendering and compute operations. In sum, Pluot resolves prior tensions between interactive performance and publication-quality figure creation, with an eye toward scientific use cases such as rendering large-scale biological datasets. The software is available at https://pluot.dev.
authorNames: Mark S Keller, Nils Gehlenborg
affiliations: Harvard Medical School

title: Human in the Loop AI Design using the Five Design-Sheets method: Supporting Reflective Visualisation and Rapid Design
abstract:
The Five Design Sheets (FDS) methodology develops strong design thinking through five stages across five sheets, progressing from multiple ideas on Sheet 1 to three refined alternatives and a final design. However, producing a full Sheet 1 often takes over an hour
to sketch, which is too long for a typical class. This work explores how generative AI can do the heavy lifting of sketching while the student stays in control of the thinking, critique and final decisions. We present a prompt framework that gives AI the FDS knowledge it
needs, investigate it across three current AI models, and outline an early classroom workflow in which the student remains the designer. Our early results suggest that structured prompting substantially improves the quality and structure of AI-generated FDS sheets —and that the structured brief, not the choice of model, drives the improvement. We report this as early work in progress.
authorNames: Rafi Ullah Tori, Panagiotis D. Ritsos, Peter W. S. Butcher, Jonathan C Roberts
affiliations: Bangor University

title: Peak-a-boo: Making Binary Chromatographic Peak Detections Reviewable
abstract: Chromatographic peak detectors return binary decisions, even though smoothing, local noise, signal overlap, and parameter choices can affect the outcomes. This sensitivity complicates interpretation and may encourage over-reliance on automation. We present Peak-a-boo, an uncertainty-aware visual analytics workbench that combines segment-dependent detection with evidence for detectability, perturbation stability, reference correspondence, and provenance in a review and audit workflow. On six synthetic chromatograms with 84 reference intervals, segment-dependent filtering removed 23.4% of unsupported detections while retaining all supported peaks. Across 105 parameter configurations, the best setting achieved F₁ = 0.950, and detectability separated supported from unsupported candidates more clearly than stability. Peak-a-boo demonstrates how complementary algorithmic evidence can support the review of uncertain scientific detections.
authorNames: Saurav Ghosh, Saugat Pandey, Alvitta Ottley
affiliations: Furman University, Washington University in St. Louis

title: Agency Over Transparency: Empirical Evidence for the Understanding-Trust Gap in AI-Assisted Camouflage Analysis
abstract: Explainable AI assumes a simple chain: transparency produces understanding, and understanding produces trust. We empirically debunked this assumption. In a controlled study (N = 150) comparing two AI-assisted camouflage detection interfaces, users who fully understood how a system worked still did not trust it. This understanding-trust gap persisted across all conditions. Adding interactive explainability produced a very large effect on perceived agency (d = 1.19) but only a small effect on trust (d = 0.33) and no effect on understanding (d = -0.02). Agency increased substantially while trust improved only marginally. We introduce the Mixed-Initiative Camouflage Analysis (MICA) framework, which repositions structured user control rather than transparency as the operative mechanism for trust calibration.
authorNames: Debra L Hogue, Ghulam Jilani Quadri
affiliations: University of Oklahoma

title: Blooming Vowels: Visualizing Four Hu and Emotional Expression in Mandopop Lyrics
abstract: This work explores the relationship between phonology and emotion in Mandopop lyrics from 1991 to 2025. Instead of treating phonetic structure and emotion as abstract concepts, we leverage linguistic analysis and data visualization to render them visible and interactive. Grounded in the traditional Four Hu phonological system, we analyze the distribution of vowel categories, the emotional tendencies of lyrics at both the word level and song level, and the potential relationship between phonetic patterns and emotional expression across different time periods. We present the data findings through an interactive 3D flower visualization interface, demonstrating a unique visualization approach to understanding how pronunciation and emotion interplay in song lyrics.
authorNames: Jiayi Sun, Xiaoyu Zhang
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong

title: MEanings: Visualizing Multimodal Wellbeing Data through a Colour-Pictorial Dashboard for Holistic Reflection
abstract: Digital wellbeing tools increasingly help people record mood, behaviour, and reflections, yet often reduce these rich qualitative records to scores, streaks, or simplified charts. We present MEanings, an early-stage colour-pictorial dashboard that visualises multimodal wellbeing data while preserving personal meaning. Informed by Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT), MEanings organises input across body, thoughts, emotions, and behaviours, and represents patterns through user-defined colour palettes, body pictograms, and calendar-based summaries. Rather than relying on fixed colour-emotion mappings, people define colours according to their own emotional associations. We outline the design rationale, prototype, and planned evaluation of support for holistic reflection and pattern recognition.

authors.name: Ana Marques
authors.affiliation: City St George's University of London

authors.name: Narges Mahyar
authors.affiliation: City St George’s, University of London

authorNames: Ana Marques, Sabah Azhar, Narges Mahyar
affiliations: City St George's University of London, City St Georges, City St George’s, University of London

title: A Visual Approach to Auditing Cross-Lingual Attribution Bias in LLMs
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly consulted as informal knowledge sources, yet the answer a model gives can depend on the emph{language} the question is asked in. We present an interactive lab that probes this cross-lingual divergence by asking the same factual question in several languages across several models, reducing each free-text answer to a canonical cited entity, and surfacing where the attributions disagree. The system contributes (i) a reproducible generate-extract-cluster pipeline that turns multilingual prose into comparable entity citations; (ii) two interpretable metrics, Core Answer Flexibility (CAF) and Context Richness (CR), that separate whether the headline answer changes from whether alternatives are acknowledged; and (iii) four coordinated views for reading bias at a glance. Across two probes, "Who invented the airplane?" and "Who invented the telephone?", in three to four languages over seven models, we find cross-lingual bias rarely flips the main answer; instead, it surfaces in the also-cited periphery, and the sharpest axis separating models is whether they acknowledge alternatives at all.
authorNames: Priscylla Silva
affiliations: IFAL

title: X-Raying a Research Institute: An interactive visual analytics system for exploring a research center's teams, topics, and collaborations over time
abstract: We present a visual analytics system for exploring data about research teams at a public French research institute. Research institute managers need to make strategic decisions about team creation, hiring, and restructuring, but the data they need is scattered across administrative databases, publication repositories, and annual reports. Our tool is ultimately meant to help managers make these decisions, but can also support communication about the institute more broadly. We conducted a requirements analysis with eight members of a center management committee. Based on these requirements, we integrate four data sources, compute data-driven research profiles from publication venues, and provide linked views with temporal filtering and bubble-set overlays. We describe the tool design, its data pipeline, and the findings from our requirements analysis.
authorNames: Olha Baliasina, Petra Isenberg, Jean-Daniel Fekete
affiliations: Inria Saclay, Université Paris-Saclay, CNRS, Inria, Université Paris-Saclay, CNRS, Inria, LISN

title: Beyond Turns: Fragment-Response Alignment for Evolving Intent and Traceable Review in LLM Chat
abstract: LLM chat interfaces are increasingly used for complex tasks, yet remain tethered to rigid, chronological transcripts. This structure creates a "traceability gap," hindering users from mapping evolving intent to fragmented model outputs. In this work, we introduce Fragment-Response Alignment, a conceptual framework that maps user intent fragments to specific AI response units. We report findings from a formative study of 16 participants, which reveal three core phenomena: intent is continuously evolving, interaction functions as a traceability reconstruction task, and users naturally employ fragment-based mental models.
authorNames: Xichun Xu, Ruofei Du, Jiaqi Zheng, Qingping Wang, Lijie Yao, Liu YANG
affiliations: Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University, Xi’an Jiaotong-Liverpool University

title: VizSync: Supporting Interactive Audience Exploration in Data-Rich Presentations
abstract: Visualizations are widely used to communicate analytical findings during presentations, yet the transition from interactive analysis environments to presentation formats often reduces them to static artifacts. We present VizSync, a presentation-oriented visualization system designed to support shared interaction and insight exchange between presenters and audiences during live data-rich presentations. VizSync enables audience members to independently interact with visualizations, capture and annotate the visualization states underlying their observations, and submit these states to the presenter for selective incorporation into the presentation. The presenter can review audience-generated views and selectively incorporate them into the presentation display while maintaining narrative control. We illustrate the use of the system through a case study involving an interactive digital health presentation, demonstrating how audience-generated, annotated visualization states can be incorporated into live discussion. By enabling parallel exploration, annotation, and state-based sharing of insights, VizSync demonstrates how presentations can move from one-way information delivery toward shared sensemaking activities around data.
authorNames: Matthew Klich, Jillian Aurisano
affiliations: University of Cincinnati

title: From Model Disagreement to Reusable Evidence: Human-in-the-Loop Visual Adjudication for Multi-Model Timing-Diagram Parsing
abstract: Timing diagrams combine waveform structures, textual annotations, and protocol assumptions, making their semantics difficult for multimodal models to interpret consistently. Models may disagree on sampling conditions, signal roles, and validity intervals, while conventional aggregation hides the evidence behind these differences. We present a human-in-the-loop visual adjudication workflow that structures model outputs as comparable claims, reveals competing interpretations and their evidence, and supports expert review. Adjudicated cases are further summarized as reusable accepted and rejected reasoning patterns. A case study with two cryptographic hardware specifications illustrates claim-level disagreement resolution and selective cross-document experience reuse.
authorNames: Yaping Liu, Shenghan Gao, Quan Li
affiliations: ShanghaiTech University

title: Allocating the Diameter Budget: Task-Aware Bubble Size Emphasis under Fixed Layout Constraints
abstract: While bounding bubble diameters helps prevent chart and map occlusion, standard scaling often treats these limits passively. We reframe the fixed size range as a proactive design choice and finite visual budget. Rather than relying on a static, task-blind curve, the strategy lets designers allocate pixel resolution based on user scenarios: exposing subtle variation among dense small values or accentuating gaps between top-end values.
authorNames: Kedi Zhang
affiliations: N/A

title: Visualization Literacy in United States Classrooms: A Qualitative Analysis of State Standards for K–12 Education Policy
abstract: Visualization literacy—the ability to interpret, reason about, and communicate information through visual representations of data—plays a critical role in decision-making, civic participation, and STEM learning. Prior research has primarily examined it through assessment frameworks, educational interventions and materials, and studies of public understanding, but comparatively little is known about how these skills are formally introduced throughout primary and secondary education (K–12) in the United States. State learning standards describe the knowledge and skills students are expected to acquire across grades and subjects, offering a unique perspective into educational expectations surrounding visualization literacy. We compiled STEM education standards from all 50 U.S. states and extracted 4,872 visualization-related standards from a representative subset of 20, each coded by visualization task, idiom, representation mode, grade level, and subject. Preliminary findings show instruction progresses from concrete representations and retrieval-based tasks toward more abstract forms and analytical reasoning. This work contributes a large-scale corpus of policy-derived visualization literacy standards and a foundation for connecting visualization literacy theory with formal educational practice.
authorNames: Julia Weppler, Mackenzie Michael Creamer, Michelle A. Borkin
affiliations: Northeastern University

title: Enriching Practice Understanding for Leisure-Time Squash Players
abstract: Squash is widely played for fitness and enjoyment, yet many leisure-time players practice without professional coaching or structured feedback. Because rallies unfold quickly, players may struggle to follow the ball, judge shot validity, identify decisive moments, and recall what happened after a session. Practice videos can support review, but raw footage often remains difficult to interpret. In this poster, we present an exploratory study on enriching squash practice videos to support leisure-time players’ understanding of their own practice. We gathered feedback from squash players to identify key review needs, including ball visibility, trajectory, court areas, shot validity, and rally-level summaries. Based on these needs, we designed video-based visual and auditory cues, such as ball highlights, trajectory traces, court-area guidance, shot indicators, and brief post-rally summaries. We embedded these cues into recorded first-person squash practice videos and used them as probes to examine how players interpret and reflect on their practice. Our work highlights opportunities for making squash practice more understandable and helpful for leisure-time players.
authorNames: Xi Zhou, Junhao Zhao, Liu YANG, Lijie Yao
affiliations: Xi'an Jiaotong Liverpool University, Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University

title: Do OpenVLA Transformers Encode Motion Primitives? A Layer-wise Attention Analysis
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models such as OpenVLA have demonstrated strong performance in robotic manipulation by jointly modeling visual observations and action generation. In this work, we investigate whether specific hidden layers specialize in distinct motion primitives during manipulation. We use a layer-wise attention visualization method over OpenVLA and analyze action sequences from egocentric manipulation datasets. Through the analysis of different motion stages at different depths, our findings suggest that the motion primitive is not explicitly constructed, but rather emerges naturally through hierarchical transformer representations, providing new interpretability insights for embodied foundation models.
authorNames: Yuanzhe Jin, Qiong Wang, Yiwen Xing
affiliations: Northwestern University, University of Oxford

title: ProGram: A Grammar for Progressive Visualization Pipelines
abstract:
Progressive Visual Analytics (PVA) systems have demonstrated the effectiveness of time-bounded, incremental computation for exploring large-scale data. 
However, PVA implementations are often difficult to reuse and extend because their progressive behaviors are typically implemented through ad hoc, hard-coded mechanisms distributed across servers and clients.
To address this limitation, we present ProGram, a grammar for progressive visualization. 
ProGram is designed not only to support core progressive features while reducing implementation burden, but also to extend the design space by introducing novel mechanisms, such as lockstepping and temporal prioritization to better support diverse usage scenarios. 
Finally, we demonstrate the utility of ProGram by reproducing progressive visualization systems.
authorNames: SeungHoon Jung, Jaemin Jo
affiliations: Sungkyunkwan University

title: PlotWise: Exploring Instruction-Practice Alignment in Interactive Visualization Learning
abstract:
Scatterplots are widely used to teach and communicate relationships between quantitative variables. However, students often misunderstand key concepts such as correlation strength and regression slope, frequently conflating the two. We present PlotWise, a
web-based interactive scatterplot learning environment developed
through collaboration between visualization researchers and learning scientists. We report a preliminary 2 × 2 between-subjects online study (N= 80), crossing instruction type (PlotWise-integrated vs. static) with practice type (PlotWise interactive vs. static) to examine effects on conceptual learning and situational interest. Results suggest that PlotWise may be most useful as an interactive learning environment when students have first seen the system used to explain the underlying concepts during instruction. However,
broader conceptual learning and interest measures did not show consistent condition differences, so we interpret the findings as exploratory rather than conclusive evidence of learning gains. This poster uses PlotWise to examine how interactive visualization practice should be connected to instruction, scaffolding, and assessment in statistics learning.
authorNames: Jiarong Feng, Karen Bonilla, Stacy Shaw, Icy(Yunyi) Zhang, Lane Harrison
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison, Worcester Polytechnic Institute

title: Trade-offs in Data Color Palette Design Tools
abstract: Designing a color palette for data requires designers to balance multiple constraints, including accessibility and aesthetics. Color palette tools support this process through features including direct manipulation, automated palette generation and evaluation, previews, and so on. Despite their prominence,  relatively little is known about how these different mechanisms shape design across contexts. We conducted an exploratory think-aloud crowd work study with 40 self-identified designers. Each participant used one of four palette tools selected to span different interaction modalities to complete a series of accessibility- and aesthetics-oriented design tasks. We observed two preliminary patterns. First, tool differences were more pronounced in accessibility-constrained tasks. Second, even when accessibility was not explicitly required, some tools produced more accessibility-friendly palettes and prompted more accessibility-oriented thinking. In this tool genre, then, system design shapes outcomes both via built-in functionality, as well as by directing designers' attention toward particular constraints and design considerations.
authorNames: Shiyi He, Andrew M McNutt
affiliations: University of Utah

title: The Met Origins: A Spatial Discovery Interface for Connecting Audiences to Museum Objects Through Space and Time
abstract: Museum collections worldwide are overwhelmingly organized by department, medium, or period, so where an object came from, and the journey it took to arrive, is rarely a way into the collection at all. We present the Met Origins, a web-based interactive that maps 6,008 geocoded objects from The Metropolitan Museum of Art's open-access collection to their places of origin. Rather than supporting retrieval of a known item, the interface is designed for discovery: users spin a 3D globe, filter across five millennia, and trace the documented routes individual objects took to reach New York. The same data is offered as both individual points and an aggregated hex-bin density view, so an apparent pattern can be checked against the underlying records rather than taken on trust. We describe the design and the structure it surfaces, including geographic concentrations and absences that reflect the institution's own collecting history rather than world art history. We frame, and propose to evaluate, whether this spatial, exploration-first approach helps general audiences perceive that structure.
authorNames: Kshitija Chandra Tammireddi, Kanishka Balaji Baskar
affiliations: Pratt Institute, University of Washington

title: Philosophical Lenses on Data Visualization
abstract: Data visualization treats visual insight as its fundamental research object, drawing on  computer science, perceptual studies, and cognition. But producing insight means producing truth and knowledge, which philosophy has studied for millennia. Despite this, only a fraction of work at IEEE VIS and TVCG draws explicitly on philosophical sources. In his 2025 VIS keynote, Hans-Christian Hege argued that elevating visualization to a science requires a philosophical foundation. We note that philosophical commitments already permeate VIS papers implicitly. Some of these commitments are revealed by the language these papers use. As an exploratory study, we build a lexicon for the five primary branches of philosophy from the Internet Philosophy Ontology (InPhO) and score every IEEE VIS abstract from 1990 to 2024 using BM25. We then examine the distribution of papers across the branches split by VIS submission area and its progression year by year. Metaphysics leads and aesthetics follows, though largely through borrowed data-modeling vocabulary, and over three decades the field drifts toward epistemology and ethics.
authorNames: Stefan Matei Cobeli, Gustavo Moreira
affiliations: University of Illinois Chicago, University of Illinois at Chicago

title: Tracing Communicative Motive in LLM-Generated Visualizations: An Activity-Theory-Informed Artifact Analysis
abstract: LLM-based visualization workflows can translate broad prompts into data transformations, analysis code, and visual encodings [2,5], but this automation makes human-specified communicative motives difficult to trace. We examine this traceability problem through a work-in-progress artifact analysis of an Activity-Theory-grounded prompting workflow [4]. Across three public datasets and three intended VisAct motives—Inform, Provoke, and Discover—we generated 135 Vega-Lite visualizations using three frontier LLMs and coded 269 visual components [3]. Each component was analyzed by composition strategy, insight need, visual form, claim, rhetoric with codes adapted from visualization task typologies, the nested model, VisActs, and visualization rhetoric [1, 3, 6, 7]. The resulting patterns suggest that motive conditions are associated with different artifact-level design pathways and recurring misalignments among motive, insight need, form, and framing. We contribute an exploratory coding workflow for studying communicative motive realization in LLM-generated visualizations.
authorNames: Divya Prasanth Paraman, Katy Börner
affiliations: Indiana University, Indiana University Bloomington

title: JITVis: A Phase-based Visualization for Intermediate Representations in JIT Compilers
abstract: Web browsers rely on Just-In-Time (JIT) compilers to optimize JavaScript execution. JIT compilers improve the performance of input bytecode through a sequence of optimization phases. JIT compilers often use an intermediate representation (IR), such as an IR graph, to track code dependencies in these optimization phases. Compiler bugs can corrupt these IR graphs, risking accuracy and security. While current debugging tools visualize single optimization phases, they struggle with multi-phase, cross-run analysis. We propose JITVis, a phase-based visualization tool that enables direct comparison of two phases and an overview of all phases in all code runs. We validate our prototype through a case study and are iteratively refining the tool with domain experts.
authorNames: Kwasi Buansi, Olivia Burls, Ellora Devulapally, Taft Harrell, HeuiChan (Terrence) Lim, Katy P Williams
affiliations: Davidson College

title: Echo: Visual Steering for AI-Assisted Cohort Definition and Comparison in Electronic Health Records
abstract: Constructing clinical cohorts in Electronic Health Records (EHRs) requires translating clinical eligibility intent into executable database logic while preserving assumptions and downstream effects. Large language model (LLM)-based query generation can reduce SQL authoring barriers, but offers limited support for inspecting how criteria are grounded, refined, and compared across alternative cohort definitions. We present Echo, an early-stage visual analytics prototype for steering AI-assisted cohort construction in EHRs. Echo combines an editable Criteria Graph, criterion-level SQL review, and coordinated cohort comparison views. A case study with two domain experts suggests that Echo has the potential to support eligibility-logic inspection and sub-cohort derivation, while surfacing needs for codelist validation, value-based variables, temporal logic, and larger-scale evaluation.
authorNames: Ruey-Ling Weng, Vincent J. Zhang, Lingfei Qian, Vipina K. Keloth, Yujia Zhou, Na Hong, Hua Xu, Huan He
affiliations: Yale University

title: The LLM Belief Atlas: Visualizing How Language-Model Stances Depend on Elicitation
abstract: What a language model appears to believe about a proposition is not a scalar but a signal that depends on how it is elicited and read: forcing a choice can fabricate a value, option-logprob scoring carries order bias, and sycophancy makes a stance a function of framing. We present the LLM Belief Atlas, a scalable in-browser WebGL instrument organized around a framework of belief spaces. The framework treats a model's stance as a latent construct observed only through a four-dimensional measurement space, model, item, elicitation condition, and readout channel, and names seven subspaces, each bound to a facet of psychometric construct validity. The instrument co-registers three switchable belief readouts (Likert agreement, free-text reflection, and option logprobs) of the same elicitation instances and morphs between them at the million-point scale, while exposing uncertainty. On 76,048 elicited beliefs from four LLMs, framing conditions explain a share of stance variance comparable to belief itself (27.1% vs 35.9%, and larger on the two natively-read models), and a within-model reliability measure predicts when cross-model disagreement is reproducible.
authorNames: Fan Huang
affiliations: Indiana University Bloomington

title: From Visual Multiplexing to Zebra Maps
abstract:
Visual multiplexing refers to the simultaneous presentation of multiple pieces of information associated with the same spatial location. By leveraging human perceptual and cognitive capabilities, viewers can often de-multiplex multiple visual signals from a
shared representation. Despite its widespread presence in visualization, the deliberate use of multiplexing as a design strategy remains underexplored. This poster presents an ongoing investigation of multiplexing through a case study in machine learning workflows for solving partial differential equations (PDEs). In this application context, researchers frequently compare multiple spatially aligned scalar fields, making it difficult to identify local relationships using conventional juxtaposed visualizations. Building upon a collection of multiplexed representations, we explore layered designs that combine heatmaps, contours, glyphs, and a novel Zebra Map representation. Zebra Maps introduce contour-like value boundaries into dense scalar fields while preserving heatmap patterns, enabling
more effective comparison between aligned fields. Through collaboration with PDE experts, we continue to refine multiplexing strategies and are developing an interactive visualization environment for constructing and exploring multiplexed visualizations.
authorNames: Yiwen Xing, Afrah Farea, Saiful Khan, Min Chen
affiliations: Istanbul technical University, Science and Technology Facilities Council, University of Oxford

title: A Geospatial Visualization Framework for Large Displays
abstract: Large High-Resolution Displays (LHRDs) provide immense visual space and pixel density, making them highly effective for collaborative, data-intensive spatial analysis. However, seamlessly combining complex geospatial analysis and natural user interactions within a unified, real-time architecture remains an open challenge. This poster presents a geospatial visualization and interaction framework for LHRDs. Our system integrates web maps, computer vision-driven mid-air gestures, and a lightweight language model. Initial user feedback during a terrain-aware risk-assessment case study highlights that the combination of embodied interaction and natural language AI significantly increases engagement and collaborative workflow efficiency compared to traditional input methods.
authorNames: Jalal Safari Bazargani, Soo-Mi Choi
affiliations: Sejong University

title: Factories, Flowers, and Trees: Visual Metaphors of People’s AI Mental Models
abstract: Despite efforts to build AI literacy programs for laypeople, solutions often overlook their existing perceptions and mental models of AI, which can play an important role in shaping how literacy programs are designed and taught. People's mental models of AI influence how they react to and engage with these systems, but they are difficult to capture. While studies in human-centered computing have relied on proxy or explicit techniques to capture mental models in human-AI interaction contexts, we focus on implicitly capturing and analyzing mental models through an open-ended design activity in which participants physicalize and visualize their understanding of AI using tangible materials such as Legos and Play-Doh. We conducted a workshop in which participants worked individually and in groups to build physical and/or visual representations of AI through design activities and educational interventions. We also administered pre- and post-surveys to gauge changes in participant perceptions. We found that participants' mental models of AI drew on analogies and metaphors, and extended beyond the commonly assumed ``black box'' framing. In this poster, we present a qualitative coding of participants' visual representations of AI, cataloging the themes and elements that appeared before and after our interventions.
authorNames: Shani Claire Spivak, Lucy Havens, Mahsan Nourani
affiliations: Northeastern University

title: An expressive, flexible railroad layout engine
abstract: Railroad layout is a style of graph layout for an extension of directed series-parallel graphs that allows some cycles. Railroad layout is commonly used for visualizing formal grammars; we outline our in-progress approach to building a railroad layout engine that can express more of the rich variation in hand-drawn layouts and give the user more fine-grained control than any existing algorithm, extending our own prior work. Further, we claim that railroad layout can apply to other domains with similar structure, such as pretty-printing code and visualizing structured control-flow graphs. We describe how we plan to evaluate our claims. We are eager to present and receive feedback on visualization work that so far has largely been limited to the programming languages community.
authorNames: Shardul Chiplunkar, Clément Pit-Claudel
affiliations: EPFL

title: Visualizing Dengue Forecasts for Public Health Preparedness
abstract: Forecasting infectious disease outbreaks is not only a modelling challenge but also a visualization challenge. Public health practitioners must interpret forecasts, compare them with historical trends, and identify emerging outbreak hotspots to support timely interventions. We present a visual analytics system developed within the Dengue Advanced Readiness Tools (DART) project. Designed with Ho Chi Minh City Center for Disease Control (HCDC) stakeholders, the system integrates dengue surveillance data, machine learning forecasts, and historical reference data into a coordinated spatiotemporal interface. The system supports city-level forecasting, district-level comparison, uncertainty-aware exploration, and linked spatial-temporal analysis of dengue dynamics. The prototype is deployed on the infrastructure of Oxford University Clinical Research Unit (OUCRU) and is undergoing pilot evaluation with HCDC. The system also highlights opportunities for visual analytics to support epidemiological model development.
authorNames: Yiwen Xing, Tuyen Huynh, Abhishek Dasgupta, Iago Perez Fernandez, Manh Nguyen, Moritz Kraemer, Marc Choisy, David Wallom, Sophie Yacoub, Sarah Sparrow, Min Chen
affiliations: Oxford University Clinical Research Unit, Oxford University Clinical Research Unit (OUCRU), University of Oxford

title: The Effect of Visual Mark Arrangement on Value Estimation Accuracy in Waffle Charts
abstract: This study investigates whether visual mark arrangement, color ordering, and data grouping affect estimation accuracy in waffle charts with a two-value containment structure. Data from 73 participants who completed a 12-condition within-subject study were analyzed using mixed-effects multinomial logistic regression. Visual mark arrangement and color ordering showed no statistically significant effects, whereas data grouping significantly affected accuracy. Participants performed more accurately when the two quantities differed substantially and estimated the smaller contained value more accurately than the larger containing value. These findings indicate that relationships between data magnitudes may affect quantitative perception more strongly than the tested visual design variations.
authorNames: Dheerissara Lertpiriyasap, Puripant Ruchikachorn
affiliations: Chulalongkorn University

title: Visualizing the Silence: Design Challenges in Representing Asymmetric, Sparse Outcome Data
abstract: Job search applications generate data dominated by non-response, yet most tracking tools treat silence as a residual category indistinguishable from rejection. Using two personal job search datasets comprising 352 combined applications, we show that 70% received no response, all responses arrived within seven days or not at all, and referral applications produced a 5x higher response rate than cold applications. We propose two visual encodings that make silence visible and measurable, and argue that open versus closed shapes offer a lightweight, generalizable convention for distinguishing resolved outcomes from ongoing ambiguity, with implications for any domain where non-response dominates.
authorNames: Kanishka Balaji Baskar, Kshitija Chandra Tammireddi
affiliations: Pratt Institute, University of Washington

title: Towards Better Point Cloud Visualizations for Tree Segmentations
abstract: Instance segmentation of 3D forest point clouds is essential for applications such as forest monitoring, but dense canopy structure, heavy occlusion, and limited ground truth make quality assessment difficult. In practice, experts still need to visually inspect automated tree segmentations, yet conventional 3D views do not adequately support this task. This poster presents a design space for visualizing individual tree segmentations, organized around the key challenges of reducing occlusion, exposing relationships between segmented trees and neighboring points, and preserving global forest context. Our goal is to better support qualitative evaluation of segmentation quality in real-world forest point cloud data.
authorNames: Adam Niemczura, Mahsa Partovi, Dongyun Han, Federico Iuricich
affiliations: Clemson University

title: A Spatiotemporal Interface Integrating ML Chemical Classification and Orbital Dynamics for Saturn Ring-Plane Dust from the NASA Cassini Mission
abstract:
From 1999 to 2017, the Cosmic Dust Analyzer (CDA) aboard
NASA’s Cassini spacecraft recorded 2.8 million hypervelocity dust
impacts within Saturn’s E-ring and outer ring planes [ 2]. These im-
pacts yielded time-of-flight (TOF) mass spectra containing chemical
composition data. Historically, extracting chemical structural pat-
terns required a manual calibration process wherein domain experts
visually mapped raw time-of-flight peaks to chemical masses via
the standard t = α√m + t0 relationship. This manual bottleneck
limited comprehensive chemical inventories to isolated, small-scale
subsets of the data. The DustMAP (Dust Mass Analysis Pipeline) was developed to
overcome this. With convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and
random forest classifiers, DustMAP automated peak detection and
calibration optimization via weighted least squares to favor highly
precise lower-mass correlations. This machine learning advance-
ment has currently produced an analytical catalog of just over 35,000
highly precise, mass-calibrated spectra sorted into 14 distinct chemi-
cal sub-types and 4 overarching molecular families (water ice, or-
ganics, sodium/salt, and rocky/stream particles) [1].
However, presenting this data solely as a static, multi-dimensional
tabular matrix can have a context barrier. Planetary science inves-
tigations depend on knowing where and when specific chemical
species exist in relation to Saturn’s dynamic environment and active
moons (e.g., Enceladus). We present an interactive web interface
built on Svelte and Canvas 2D that integrates these ML chemical
classifications with real-time Keplerian orbital dynamics projections.
Our interface provides synchronous cross-sectional, top-down or-
bital, and global particle map views, coupled with dynamic temporal
filtering.We validate this approach through a use case in which the
interface surfaced an anomalous spatial cluster, leading to the discov-
ery of a historical reporting mismatch in legacy NASA databases.
authorNames: Lauren Pryor, Hillary Mushkin, Santiago V Lombeyda
affiliations: California Institute of Technology, California Institute of Technology (Caltech)

title: Lost in Translation: Visualizing Cultural Bias in AI Semantic Space
abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) encode language as high-dimensional vectors—a process that is both powerful and opaque. We ask whether the embeddings of abstract value concepts diverge across languages, and whether such divergence can be made visible. Using text-embedding-3-small, we embed 20 culturally loaded value concepts in English, Chinese, Spanish, and Russian, and convert the cosine similarity of each translation to its
English baseline into an angular displacement we call Cross-lingual Semantic Embedding Divergence (CSED). We map CSED onto the branch angles of L-System trees rendered in TouchDesigner, with branch thickness encoding each language’s training-data share. Russian diverges most (mean 65.2◦), Spanish least (42.1◦), and emotionally loaded concepts drift farther than institutional ones. The work makes algorithmic bias perceptible to non-technical audiences and frames it as a property of skewed training data rather than of “true” meaning.
authorNames: Han Zhang
affiliations: ArtCenter College of Design

title: Bringing Journaling Data to Life: Designing Data Characters for the Emotional Self
abstract: Journaling is a common practice for emotional expression, reflection, and processing. However, as entries accumulate, it can become difficult to interpret and compare their affective content, especially since traditional text-based analyses and visualizations often struggle to convey affective nuance. We introduce Data Characters, a visualization approach that represents affective content in journaling through human-like characters. Using a customizable Data Character as a design probe, we investigate the potential of character-based representations for conveying affective experiences and explore what visual encodings emerge through customization. Preliminary walkthroughs with two participants demonstrate the intuitiveness and feasibility of the approach. This work contributes an exploratory approach to studying how affective experiences can be visually represented and encoded through anthropomorphic forms.
authorNames: Diego Alexander Abarcar-Calugay, Isabella Amador, Keke Wu
affiliations: University of Maryland, University of Maryland - College Park, University of Maryland College Park

title: Quick-View Takeaways: How Does Title Framing Influences Pattern Identification in Line Charts?
abstract:
Visual data communication in digital media is increasingly characterized by short attention spans and snapshot-based viewing, often employing line charts to convey trends and patterns. Among all visual elements, titles are crucial elements that can shape how viewers interpret visual information and form chart takeaways. In this study, we examine how title characteristics, particularly title word count and intended message, influence people’s pattern identification in single-class line charts. Participants viewed 50 line charts
collected from online news media and identified the pattern they perceived. Our results demonstrate that both title word count and intended message significantly influence viewers’ pattern identification. Our findings highlight the importance of title framing in shaping quick-view pattern takeaways and supporting effective visualization communication.
authorNames: Jasmine Lim, Tapendra Pandey, Arran Zeyu Wang, Ghulam Jilani Quadri
affiliations: University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill, University of Oklahoma

title: PyProgressive: A Lightweight Library for Progressive Computations
abstract:
Progressive computation has emerged as a promising paradigm for handling large datasets by providing early, intermediate results within bounded response times.
However, transforming existing sequential computations into their progressive counterparts often requires substantial manual effort and algorithmic restructuring.
To address this gap, we present PyProgressive, a Python library for specifying and executing progressive computations.
With PyProgressive, users can express their computations using a simple set of sequential-style primitives, while the system automatically compiles these primitives into a form that can be updated and evaluated progressively.
We demonstrate the utility of PyProgressive through statistical and visualization tasks, including the progressive group-wise proportions.
