title: From Design Guidelines to Readability: Comparing Draco 2 with Human Judgments
abstract: We discuss the results of a comparison between human judgments of visualization readability and an automatic assessment based on empirically-derived design guidelines. The result of this comparison is important for understanding how automated applications of empirically derived guidelines might complement subjective human judgments. To achieve this goal, we compare scores from Draco 2, a comprehensive test suite that includes an underlying model of visualization guidance, against subjective participant scores from the PREVis Layout readability scale. Our results show that the automatic scores were not a good predictor of human judgment of layout readability.

title: VideoMaster: Directing Data Videos with Cinematic Narrative
abstract: Data videos combine animated charts, voiceover, and scene transitions to communicate data insights. However, effective data videos require more than presenting visual facts but demand narrative strategies to engage audiences. Existing automated generation systems express narrative intent mainly through prompts, producing narratively flat videos. We present VideoMaster, a data video generation system that introduces explicit cinematic narrative control: ten film-inspired narrative patterns, VideoSpec (a declarative narrative-state representation), and a two-stage narrative orchestration workflow. A within-subject pilot (N = 6) shows improved engagement (Mdn 5.6 vs. 3.2) and recall (88% vs. 64%) over a narrative-disabled ablation, without reducing perceived credibility.

title: A Declarative Specification for Clinical Reference Range Number Line Visualizations
abstract: Reference range number lines (RRNLs) place a single health datum on a continuous, categorically classified scale, improving comprehension of health information for at-risk patients. Despite their value, RRNLs lack a formal definition and dedicated authoring tools, so researchers build them manually. We introduce a domain-specific language (DSL) that specifies the core components of RRNLs and compiles to Vega-Lite, Vega, and (for gradients) D3. To demonstrate it, we replicate a key prior result in health communication using stimuli generated entirely from our specification, reproducing the original study’s main trends. We discuss how a visualization-grounded DSL advances accessibility, replicability, and robustness over manual RRNL creation.

title: Visualizing “Our Neighborhood Walk”: what can storymaps tell us about human-canine-environment interactions?
abstract: The “Our Neighborhood Walk” project explores how using personal geo-enabled tracking devices and interactive storymaps can advance understanding of the shared experiences and emotional connections between pet guardians and their companion dogs while walking together. We employ personal visual storytelling design techniques to unlock new insights into how humans and canines collectively and individually perceive elements of the built and natural environment. By cartographically recreating the dynamic, co-constructed sense-of-place that evolves during a routine walk, we aim to facilitate greater awareness of human-canine-environment interactions and prompt critical reflection on how to enhance those interactions in the future.

title: An Exploratory Pilot Study of the Effectiveness of XAI Visual Explanations for Novice Users
abstract: Most visual analytics tools for Explainable AI (XAI) are designed for domain experts, leaving a substantial gap in accessibility for broader populations. We present an exploratory study evaluating how non-expert users interact with popular interpretability techniques: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), influence functions, and ``what-if'' analysis. Utilizing a highly engaging sports statistics dataset (NFL Hall of Fame prediction), we extract four core user design goals through initial interviews. We then develop and evaluate an interactive dashboard system. Our exploratory study suggests that novice users prefer tabular data views and low-friction, interactive ``what-if'' slider adjustments over complex, aggregated visualizations like Beeswarm plots. Furthermore, we identify critical barriers to trust when model logic conflicts with user intuition, offering concrete design implications for future non-expert XAI interfaces.

title: A Design Space of Interactive Visual Interface for Generative Image Models
abstract: Interactive visual interfaces have become an important means of controlling generative image models, enabling users to manipulate generation through prompts, direct manipulation, and a range of interactions. However, existing techniques are typically presented as independent systems, making it difficult to understand how they relate, compare their interaction mechanisms, or identify opportunities for new interface designs. We introduce a design space for interactive visual interfaces for generative image models derived from 51 research systems and practitioner tools. The framework decomposes each system into three complementary components: the user interface (U), the controllable model objects (Z), and the mapping function ($phi$) that translates user interaction into model operations. This decomposition provides a common representation for analyzing heterogeneous interaction techniques across model families, revealing recurring design patterns and underexplored regions of the design space. We further present an interactive corpus explorer that support comparative analysis, and discuss usage scenarios for both educational settings and HCI/AI practitioners identifying research and design opportunities.
